Routine blood tests have a limited but real role in cancer detection, depending on cancer type and context. Aside from leukemia and other blood cancers, most cancers cannot be detected during routine blood work alone, though blood tests can provide clues about overall health, organ function, and chemicals or proteins that might indicate cancer [d1][d2]. For metastatic cancer, routine blood tests can reveal elevated liver enzymes that may suggest liver metastasis, but results are often normal even in the presence of advanced cancer [d5]. For skin cancer specifically, blood tests and imaging scans are not currently used as screening tools, though studies are underway to explore whether skin cancer DNA concentrations can be detected in blood [d7]. Research on aggressive lymphoma surveillance found that routine laboratory testing detected relapse in only 5% of relapsed patients, with a sensitivity of 42% and a positive predictive value of just 9%, concluding that routine blood tests have limited value in this context [d4][d8]. Beyond standard routine tests, specialized tools add further capability: a liquid biopsy can detect circulating tumor DNA to help identify specific genetic changes in non-small cell lung cancer, though it cannot diagnose the cancer itself [d3], and the Galleri multi-cancer early detection test can detect cancer signals across more than 50 cancer types through a routine blood draw, though it requires confirmatory diagnostic evaluation and should be used alongside other recommended screenings [d6]. In summary, routine blood tests alone are insufficient to diagnose most cancers, but they serve as one useful component of a broader diagnostic approach, and newer specialized blood tests are expanding detection capabilities.
